summary: The letter closes with instructions for life together — restore the caught one gently, bear one another's burdens and so fulfill the law of Christ, each examine their own work, share with the teacher, sow to the Spirit because God is not mocked — and then Paul takes the pen himself: large letters, his own hand, one final cut at the circumcision party's motives, and the letter's true boast — the cross, through which the world has been crucified to him and he to the world. Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is anything; what counts is a new creation.
whyItMatters: The final chapter shows the letter's freedom working at ground level — burdened people, tempted people, ordinary generosity — and then ends by putting the whole conflict in one sentence: the only thing that avails is being made new. The closing marks-on-the-body line is Paul's signature in every sense.

context.author: Paul, explicitly taking over the pen at 6:11 — 'See with what large letters I write to you with my own hand' — so the letter ends in the author's own handwriting.
context.audience: The Galatian assemblies, given not abstract freedom but instructions for how the community carries its members — the caught, the burdened, the taught, the weary.
context.date: Undated; the chapter's tone is the letter's close, with the author's physical marks (6:17) and a final blessing (6:18).
context.setting: Still the same crisis, but the camera has pulled back to ordinary assembly life — restoration, money, work, weariness — before one last strike at the agitators' motives.
context.literaryForm: Paraenesis — short, stacked instructions — closing with an autographic subscription (the author's own hand) and a final benediction.

outline.heading: Restore, bear, examine
outline.note: The spiritual restore a caught brother in gentleness, watching themselves; bear one another's burdens — 'and so fulfill the law of Christ'; self-examination instead of comparison, each carrying their own burden.

outline.heading: Sharing, sowing, not growing weary
outline.note: The taught share all good things with the teacher; God is not mocked — whatever a man sows he reaps, corruption from the flesh, eternal life from the Spirit; do good without giving up, toward all and especially the household of faith.

outline.heading: Paul's own hand and the last cut
outline.note: Large letters, his own hand; the circumcision party's motive exposed — a good impression in flesh, avoidance of persecution for the cross, boasting in the Galatians' flesh — while not keeping the law themselves.

outline.heading: The only boast and the new creation
outline.note: Boast only in the cross — the world crucified to Paul and he to the world; neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is anything, but a new creation; peace and mercy on those who walk by this rule; the marks of Jesus on his body; grace with their spirit.

keyVerses.text: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
keyVerses.why: The letter that argued against the law gives it a fulfillment — not the boundary markers, but burden-carrying love; the phrase 'the law of Christ' names where the letter's freedom points.

keyVerses.text: But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
keyVerses.why: The letter's boast inverted: what the agitators want to boast in (the Galatians' flesh, 6:13) is answered by the only boast Paul will make — a mutual crucifixion that ended both directions of claim.

keyVerses.text: For in Christ Jesus neither is circumcision anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.
keyVerses.why: The whole dispute settled in one line: the sign in flesh, in either direction, counts for nothing; what counts is being made new — the letter's last word on the question it was written to answer.

themes: burden-bearing as the law of Christ

questions.question: Who is 'a man caught in some fault' and what should happen?
questions.answer: A member of the assembly overtaken by wrongdoing — the word means caught, as in a snare. The instruction is for 'you who are spiritual' to restore, with two guards on the operation: 'in a spirit of gentleness,' and 'looking to yourself so that you also aren't tempted' (6:1). Restoration, not exclusion or contempt, is the community's reflex.

questions.question: How does bearing burdens 'fulfill the law of Christ'?
questions.answer: The letter spent chapters arguing against the law of Moses as justification, so the phrase 'the law of Christ' is striking. In this chapter's own content, the law of Christ is what 5:14 quoted — 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' — made practical: carrying what presses on another person. It is the letter's positive replacement of boundary-keeping with burden-carrying.

questions.question: Doesn't 'each man will bear his own burden' contradict 'bear one another's burdens'?
questions.answer: The two verses sit four verses apart and are the chapter's most-asked puzzle. Most readers resolve it by the two different Greek words: 6:2 uses a word for heavy loads — the kind needing helpers — while 6:5 uses a word for the pack each soldier carries, one's own accountability. The letter holds both: carry what crushes each other, and answer for your own work — 6:4's self-examination sits between them.

questions.question: What is the sowing-and-reaping instruction about?
questions.answer: 'Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap' (6:7) — applied to two fields: sowing to his own flesh reaps corruption; sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life (6:8). The context is communal generosity (6:6 sharing with the teacher; 6:10 doing good toward all), so the farming image treats ordinary choices as seeds with a certain harvest — and the reason given is theology, not technique: 'God is not mocked.'

questions.question: What does Paul mean by 'large letters' in his own hand?
questions.answer: Ancient letters were normally dictated to a scribe, with the author adding a closing line as authentication. Paul takes the pen at 6:11 — the letter's argument closes with his own handwriting, and the word for the writing (grammasin, letters) says he wrote in big, deliberate strokes. Why the letters are large is argued: bold emphasis, a poor hand, or eyesight (the same letter mentions 4:15, 'you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me'). What is not argued is the function: the author's hand on everything above.

questions.question: What does Paul say the circumcision party's motives really are?
questions.answer: Three charges at 6:12-13: they want 'a good impression in the flesh'; they aim 'that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ' — the message that Gentiles need nothing added is what got Paul persecuted (5:11); and they do not keep the law themselves but want to boast in the Galatians' flesh. The accusation reframes the debate: it was never only about fidelity to the law.

questions.question: What are 'the marks of the Lord Jesus' on Paul's body?
questions.answer: 'I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus branded on my body' (6:17) — the word is the brand or scar of a slave. Paul's body carried what following Christ had cost — he lists beatings, stonings, and scars elsewhere — and the line functions as a final credential: the man the agitators dismiss has the brand-marks of the one he serves. It is also a boundary: 'let no one cause me any trouble' — the letter closes where it began, with an authority claim.

questions.question: What does 'a new creation' mean in the final verse pair?
questions.answer: 'Neither is circumcision anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation' (6:15) — the letter's summary verdict. The two sides of the whole dispute are declared equally irrelevant, and what 'is' anything is a made-new reality. The phrase looks back to the letter's argument (crucified with Christ, the Spirit, the heir come of age) and states the result as a creation-word: something God does, not something done to flesh.

questions.question: Why does Paul say 'let no one cause me any trouble' at the very end?
questions.answer: Coming between the boast in the cross and the final blessing, the line (6:17) reads as the letter's exhausted closing guard: after six chapters of argument, Paul puts his scarred body between the readers and the agitators. Within the letter it restates the opening claim (1:1, 1:8-9) at the moment of signature — the authority question, raised in the first line, is settled in the last.

glossary.def: Paul's phrase for what the letter's freedom fulfills — burden-bearing love (6:2), matching the quoted command to love the neighbor (5:14).
The letter's final standard of what counts: not the state of a person's flesh either way, but the made-new reality in Christ (6:15).
The brand-scars of a slave; Paul's word for what his body carries from following Jesus, shown as his final credential (6:17).
